basic.title: Introduction to Programming
basic.overview: Learn to think like a computer: break a problem into small, exact steps.

lesson.title: Algorithms: instructions with no guessing
paragraphs: A computer does exactly what you tell it and nothing more. If a step is missing or unclear, it cannot fill the gap the way a person would.
An algorithm is a list of precise steps that solves a problem. Programming means writing that list in a language the machine can run.
Try the idea with a daily task, such as making a cup of tea. A person simply does it. A computer needs every step: get a cup, fill the kettle, wait for the water to boil, and so on.

basic.realWorld: Developers often turn a vague request like “make checkout faster” into precise steps a program can follow.

task.prompt: Write the steps to cook instant noodles so precisely that a robot could follow them. Do not skip anything.
task.note: There is no right answer. Notice how many tiny steps you needed. That kind of precision is what programming asks for.

medium.title: Databases
medium.overview: Learn how information is organized so programs can store and find it.

lesson.title: Tables, rows, and links
paragraphs: A database stores information in tables. Each row is one record, such as one customer, and each column is one detail, such as a name or an email.
To avoid repeating data, tables are linked. An order does not copy the customer’s details. It stores a customer ID that points to one row in the customers table.
You then ask questions called queries, like “show every order from this customer last month”, and the database finds the answer in a moment.

medium.realWorld: Almost every app, from online shops to school portals, relies on a database behind the scenes.

task.prompt: A shop wants to store customers and their orders. Which approach would you choose?
options: Copy the customer’s full details into every order
Store each customer once and give every order a customer ID
Keep everything in one long text note
task.note: Many people choose the second option because it avoids repeating data. Thinking about structure like this is a big part of database work.

deep.title: Software Project
deep.overview: See how a team turns an idea into a working product.

lesson.title: From idea to release
paragraphs: A real project starts with requirements: what should the product do, and for whom? The team splits the work into small tasks and builds in short rounds, often a week or two.
Along the way they test, fix problems, and show progress to users. Plans change, so talking clearly with teammates matters as much as writing code.
Interns usually join this process by taking small tasks, such as fixing a bug or testing a new feature.

deep.realWorld: On an internship you may join a daily stand-up meeting where each person says what they did, what is next, and what blocks them.

task.prompt: Your team has three days left and five features to build. Which would you build first, and why?
task.note: There is no right answer. Choosing what to build first, and explaining it, is a real part of project work.
